paras: The lynching of Dan Smith took place at Pulaski, Tennessee, on December 2, 1880, when a crowd seized Smith, a Black man, from the Giles County court room minutes after he was sentenced to twenty-one years in the penitentiary and hanged him from a bridge. Smith had been accused of assaulting a young white girl, and the sheriff had earlier sent him to Nashville to keep him from crowds. The case was widely reported because the mob overpowered the sheriff and his posse to take a prisoner who had already been sentenced.

According to the Pulaski Citizen, Smith was accused in October of attacking Mattie Hendricks, a twelve-year-old girl living in the family of Elder William Smith on Shoal creek, and was arrested at Rogersville, Alabama. Sheriff H. Arrowsmith put him on a train for Nashville, but at Lynnville several men took him from a deputy, and the sheriff recovered him at pistol point. That night about one hundred men rode into Pulaski and searched the jail, only to find that Smith had already been sent overland to Nashville.

A meeting of South Giles citizens on October 15 demanded Smith's return for trial and pledged not to molest him until court met. Governor Marks nonetheless held him in Nashville until the November term, and Judge McLemore told the grand jury that "mob-law is a remedy for nothing," while the Citizen warned that Smith might be "taken upon his arrival and hanged."

Smith arrived from Nashville on an afternoon train on December 2, a jury was empanelled, and he was sentenced to twenty-one years, which the papers called the extreme penalty of the law. Four taps on the court house bell then called a crowd, which entered the court room and took Smith from the sheriff and his posse. A Pulaski dispatch in the Fayetteville Observer put the mob at 800 to 1,000 men and said the officers "offered a determined resistance" before they were overpowered.

The crowd took Smith down Main street to the bridge over Richland creek at the south end of town and hanged him from a beam. Rev. William Smith, who had raised both Dan Smith and the girl, prayed for him from a wagon, and a man cried out, "This man dies for the safety of the whole people." According to the wire, the mob came from the neighborhood of the alleged crime.

No report of an inquest or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage. Two days later, six grand jurors wrote to the Pulaski Citizen that the attorney general, with the judge's backing, had held back Smith's indictment until the morning of the trial despite "the excitement in the public mind."

The Nashville wire ran the next day in Washington, New York and St. Paul, later in Sacramento, under headlines such as "Hanged by a Mob," "Strung Up Without Warning" and "Judge Lynch at Work." Its wording drifted in reprinting: the Clarke Courier said four hundred people joined the mob, and the Milan Exchange had Smith hanged "while being taken to jail." A Dakota paper reprinted it on January 1, 1881.

Tennessee papers largely approved. The Banner's Pulaski correspondent, who had not witnessed the hanging, wrote that no one was masked, that the crowd included "many of the best men in the county," and that "Everybody to-day says amen to the execution." The Fayetteville Observer headed its dispatch "A Necksecution" and "The Appropriate Ending of a Lecherous Villain." The Pulaski Herald, quoted in the Clarksville Weekly Chronicle, deplored mob violence but faulted the law for limiting the penalty to a term of years. Earlier the Pulaski Citizen, which called Smith a "Negro Monster," had counseled against lynching him "not on his account, for he more than deserves it."

The Banner correspondent and the Home Journal said Smith "submitted his case," while the Fayetteville dispatch said he pleaded guilty. Local papers described an attempted rape, while the wire gave the conviction as assault with intent to commit murder. The Citizen gave the girl's age as twelve and the Home Journal as ten, and the Home Journal placed the hanging in "the suburbs of the town" rather than at the bridge.

reader.title: Lynching of Dan Smith
bases: A crowd took Smith from the sheriff and posse in the Pulaski court room after his sentence and hanged him from a bridge (A10, A13, A7).

A mob put at hundreds or 800 to 1,000 men overpowered the sheriff and hanged Smith without authority (A13, A7), avowedly to punish the alleged assault on a white girl, which the papers held the law punished too lightly (A10, A13, A17).

The Banner's Pulaski correspondent, a separate Pulaski dispatch, the Nashville wire, the Home Journal and the Pulaski grand jurors' letter agree that Smith was taken from court and hanged (A10, A13, A7, A12, A14).

accounts.label: Nashville wire
accounts.gist: Smith was sentenced to 21 years for assault with intent to commit murder; a mob rushed the court room, overpowered the sheriff and posse, was joined by hundreds in the street and hanged him from a bridge; the mob came from the vicinity of the crime.

accounts.label: Banner's Pulaski correspondent
accounts.gist: Not an eyewitness; says the crowd, called by four taps of the court house bell, was orderly, unmasked and made up of 'many of the best men in the county', and hanged Smith from a trestle of the Richmond creek bridge.

accounts.label: Pulaski dispatch (Fayetteville Observer)
accounts.gist: Smith pleaded guilty; a mob of 800 to 1,000 overpowered a resisting sheriff and posse, took him down Main street to the Richland creek bridge, and hanged him after Rev. Wm. Smith prayed.

accounts.label: Grand jurors' letter
accounts.gist: The indictment was held back by the attorney general and judge until the morning of the trial, against some jurors' wishes, despite public excitement.

framing.detail: Headlined 'A Necksecution. The Appropriate Ending of a Lecherous Villain'; called the lynching no more terrible than 'the fiendish deed'.
The Banner correspondent stressed the crowd's orderliness and respectability and wrote that everybody said 'amen to the execution'.
The Pulaski Herald deplored mob violence but argued the law erred in limiting the penalty to a term of years.
Before the lynching the Pulaski Citizen called Smith a 'Negro Monster' and counseled against lynching only because the court was ready to act.
Distant papers ran the Nashville wire under 'Hanged by a Mob', 'Carried from Court and Hung by a Mob', 'Strung Up Without Warning' and 'Judge Lynch at Work'.
